title: Refinancing a Mortgage: When It Actually Saves You Money

seo.seoTitle: Refinancing a Mortgage: When It's Worth It
seo.metaDescription: Refinancing can lower your rate, shorten your term, or free up cash — but closing costs mean it isn't always worth it. Here's how to calculate whether it makes sense.
seo.searchIntent: Commercial/informational — homeowners deciding whether refinancing their existing mortgage makes financial sense right now

excerpt: Refinancing replaces your existing mortgage with a new one — usually to get a lower rate, shorter term, or cash out equity. It isn't automatically worth it; here's how to calculate whether it actually is.
intro:
Refinancing a mortgage means paying off your current loan with a brand-new one, ideally on better terms. People refinance to lower their interest rate, switch from an adjustable to a fixed rate, shorten their loan term to build equity faster, or tap accumulated home equity as cash.

The catch is that refinancing isn't free — it comes with its own closing costs, similar in kind to the ones paid when the original mortgage was taken out. Whether it's worth it comes down to a straightforward breakeven calculation: how long until the monthly savings outweigh the upfront cost, compared against how long you actually plan to stay in the home.
tableOfContents: How Your Credit and Equity Affect the New Rate

sections.heading: Why Homeowners Refinance
paragraphs: The most common reason is a lower available interest rate than the one on your existing loan, which directly reduces your monthly payment and total interest paid over the remaining term. Others refinance to switch from an adjustable-rate mortgage to a fixed rate for payment certainty, to shorten a 30-year loan into a 15-year term and build equity faster, or to remove private mortgage insurance once they've built enough equity.

sections.heading: The Refinance Application Process
paragraphs: A refinance follows a similar path to an original purchase mortgage: application, appraisal, income and asset verification, and underwriting, before reaching clear-to-close status. Because you already own the home, the process can sometimes move faster than a purchase, particularly if you're refinancing with your existing lender and much of your documentation is already on file, though a new appraisal is still typically required to confirm the home's current value supports the new loan amount.

Gathering your documentation — recent pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements — before starting the application, just as with a purchase mortgage, is the most effective way to keep the refinance timeline on track and avoid delays waiting on paperwork mid-process. Federal regulations also provide a three-business-day right of rescission on most refinances of a primary residence, during which you can cancel the transaction without penalty — a protection that doesn't apply to a purchase mortgage, since there's no prior owner-occupied property being refinanced. Funds aren't disbursed until the rescission period passes, which is worth factoring into your timeline if you're refinancing specifically to access cash for a time-sensitive purpose.

sections.heading: Rate-and-Term vs Cash-Out Refinance
paragraphs: A rate-and-term refinance simply replaces the existing loan with a new one at a different rate, term, or both — the loan balance stays essentially the same aside from closing costs rolled in. A cash-out refinance replaces the loan with a larger one, with the difference paid to you in cash, typically used for home improvements, debt consolidation, or other major expenses.

Cash-out refinancing increases your loan balance and, usually, your monthly payment, so it's worth comparing against other financing options — like [a personal loan](/articles/complete-guide-to-personal-loans) or a dedicated home equity line — before assuming it's the cheapest way to access the cash.

sections.heading: Calculating the Breakeven Point
paragraphs: The breakeven point is simply the total closing costs divided by your monthly savings from the new rate — the result is the number of months it takes for the refinance to pay for itself. If closing costs total $4,000 and the new rate saves $150 per month, the breakeven point is roughly 27 months.

If you plan to stay in the home well beyond that breakeven point, refinancing is typically a clear financial win. If you expect to sell or move before reaching it, the closing costs likely outweigh the savings, and refinancing probably isn't worth it right now.

sections.heading: What Refinancing Costs
paragraphs: Closing costs on a refinance typically include lender origination fees, an appraisal, title search and insurance, and recording fees — often totaling a meaningful percentage of the new loan amount, similar to a home purchase. Some lenders offer a 'no-closing-cost' refinance, which usually just rolls those costs into a slightly higher rate or the loan balance rather than eliminating them, so it's worth comparing the true long-term cost either way.

sections.heading: How Your Credit and Equity Affect the New Rate
paragraphs: The same factors that determine a purchase mortgage rate apply to a refinance: credit score, debt-to-income ratio, and — specifically for a refinance — how much equity you have in the home. More equity generally supports better rates and can help you avoid mortgage insurance on the new loan. See [mortgage interest rates](/articles/mortgage-interest-rates) for the full breakdown of what shapes the rate you're offered.

sections.heading: Refinancing to Remove PMI
paragraphs: If your home's value has risen or your original loan balance has been paid down enough that you now have at least 20% equity, refinancing into a new conventional loan can eliminate private mortgage insurance even if you didn't reach that threshold through your original payment schedule alone. Some lenders also allow PMI removal on the existing loan once you hit 20% equity without a full refinance, so it's worth checking that option first, since it avoids refinance closing costs entirely if it's available to you.

Whether refinancing specifically to remove PMI makes sense still comes down to the same breakeven math — compare the ongoing PMI cost you'd eliminate against the closing costs of a full refinance, factoring in how long you plan to stay in the home. If your only goal is eliminating PMI and your rate wouldn't otherwise improve meaningfully, it's worth weighing this option carefully against simply requesting PMI cancellation on your existing loan first. Lenders are generally required to automatically cancel PMI once your balance reaches 78% of the home's original value, but you can often request cancellation earlier, once you hit 80%, by providing evidence of your current equity position, sometimes including a new appraisal at your own expense to document a value increase that outpaced your regular amortization schedule. The cost of that appraisal is typically far less than even a single year of ongoing PMI premiums, making it a straightforward calculation once you believe your home's value has genuinely risen enough to matter, especially in a market where home values have appreciated noticeably since your original purchase or last appraisal. Whichever route you take to remove it, confirm the change actually appears on your next statement, since servicing errors around PMI cancellation are common enough to be worth double-checking rather than assuming the paperwork was processed correctly the first time, since that ongoing premium adds up meaningfully over even a few extra months of oversight.

sections.heading: When Refinancing Doesn't Make Sense
paragraphs: If you're planning to move within the next couple of years, if the new rate isn't meaningfully lower than your current one, or if a cash-out refinance would erase equity you'll need later, refinancing likely isn't the right move right now. Run the actual breakeven math before assuming a lower advertised rate automatically translates into savings for your specific situation and timeline.

sections.heading: Refinancing to Change Loan Type
paragraphs: Beyond chasing a lower rate, refinancing is also the standard path for switching loan types entirely — moving from an FHA loan to a conventional loan once you've built enough equity to avoid FHA's mortgage insurance requirement, or converting an adjustable-rate mortgage to a fixed rate for payment certainty as your risk tolerance or plans change. These structural reasons to refinance can be worth pursuing even when the rate improvement alone wouldn't clear the standard breakeven math, since the value comes from the changed loan structure itself, not purely the monthly savings.

keyTakeaways: Refinancing replaces your existing mortgage with a new one, usually for a lower rate, shorter term, or to access home equity as cash.
The breakeven point — closing costs divided by monthly savings — tells you how long it takes for a refinance to pay for itself.
If you plan to stay in the home well past the breakeven point, refinancing is typically worth it; if you'll likely move sooner, it usually isn't.
Cash-out refinances increase your loan balance and should be compared against other financing options before assuming they're the cheapest route.
Your credit score, debt-to-income ratio, and home equity all affect the rate you're offered on a refinance, just as with a purchase mortgage.
"No-closing-cost" refinances typically roll the cost into a higher rate or larger balance rather than eliminating it — compare the true long-term cost.

faq.question: How much does it cost to refinance a mortgage?
faq.answer: Closing costs on a refinance typically run a meaningful percentage of the new loan amount, covering origination, appraisal, title, and recording fees — similar in structure to the costs of an original purchase mortgage.

faq.question: How do I know if refinancing is worth it?
faq.answer: Divide your total closing costs by your expected monthly savings to find the breakeven point in months. If you plan to stay in the home longer than that, refinancing is typically worth it.

faq.question: What is a cash-out refinance?
faq.answer: A refinance where the new loan is larger than your remaining balance, with the difference paid to you in cash — commonly used for home improvements or debt consolidation, though it increases your loan balance and monthly payment.

faq.question: Can I refinance if I don't have much home equity?
faq.answer: It's possible but more limited — most conventional refinances prefer at least some equity cushion, and government-backed refinance programs may have more flexible options for borrowers with less equity.

faq.question: How soon after buying a home can I refinance?
faq.answer: It varies by loan type and lender, but many conventional loans allow refinancing after a short seasoning period, sometimes as soon as six months, though waiting for a meaningful rate improvement usually matters more than the exact timing.

faq.question: Can refinancing remove private mortgage insurance?
faq.answer: Yes, if you refinance into a conventional loan once you have at least 20% equity. Some lenders also allow PMI removal on your existing loan at that threshold without a full refinance, which is worth checking first since it avoids closing costs.

conclusion:
Refinancing is a genuinely useful tool when the math clearly works: a meaningfully lower rate, a term change that fits your goals, or cash-out access that's cheaper than the alternatives — all measured against a realistic breakeven timeline for how long you'll actually stay in the home.

Run the numbers using your specific closing cost estimate and rate offer before assuming a lower advertised rate is automatically worth it, and revisit [mortgage interest rates](/articles/mortgage-interest-rates) periodically even after you've refinanced once — the same math applies again any time conditions shift meaningfully in your favor.
